title: Double entry: reading T-accounts and the Papaluwe worked answer
body:
Objectives: place each entry on the correct side of a T-account; explain why every debit has a matching credit; open and balance the accounts for a short list of cash transactions.

Teaching: A T-account has a name on top, a Dr (debit) side on the left and a Cr (credit) side on the right. Rule from the school note: debit the receiver, credit the giver. In every entry, the account that receives value is debited and the account that gives value is credited, and the particulars column names the OTHER account. Example: when cash is paid for a machine, Machine Account is debited (it receives the machine) and Cash Account is credited (cash goes out).

Reading the figures in the original lesson: in Worked Example 1, Capital is credited and Cash is debited with N5000. The original prints the date Jan. 5 in the Capital Account but Jan. 2 in the Cash Account. The sides and amount are correct; the intended date cannot be recovered from the source, so do not guess it. In Worked Example 4 the sentence is typed "Janlo"; both accounts show Jan 10.

Worked answer to the original exercise (Papaluwe Transport Company, opening cash N15,000, Feb. 2009):
- Cash Account: Dr balance b/d 15,000; Dr Feb. 5 Felele 5,000. Cr Feb. 1 Wages 3,000; Feb. 4 Electricity 1,000; Feb. 10 Rent 500; Balance c/d 15,500. Both sides total 20,000.
- Wages Account: Dr Feb. 1 Cash 3,000.
- Electricity Account: Dr Feb. 4 Cash 1,000.
- Felele Account: Cr Feb. 5 Cash 5,000 (Felele gave the cash).
- Rent Account: Dr Feb. 10 Cash 500.
Check: 15,000 + 5,000 - 3,000 - 1,000 - 500 = 15,500. Total debits posted outside Cash (3,000 + 1,000 + 500 = 4,500) plus the credit in Felele (5,000) mirror the cash entries.

Practice questions:
1. On Mar. 2 a trader starts business with N8,000 cash. Name the account debited and the account credited.
2. On Mar. 5 he buys a typewriter for N2,500 cash. Write both T-account entries.
3. On Mar. 9 he pays N700 cash to a supplier, K. Ola. Which side of K. Ola's account is used?

Answers and marking guide: 1. Debit Cash 8,000; credit Capital 8,000. 2. Debit Typewriter Account 2,500 (Mar. 5, Cash); credit Cash Account 2,500 (Mar. 5, Typewriter). 3. The debit side of K. Ola's account (Mar. 9, Cash, 700); Cash is credited. Award one mark for each correct account and one for each correct side; total entries must equal on both sides.

title: Trial balance: checking the cash book, ledgers and the corrected second method
body:
Objectives: read a two-sided cash book; carry balances (c/d, b/d) into a trial balance; check that debits equal credits; recognise the missing line in the original second-method example.

Teaching: A trial balance lists every ledger balance in a Dr column or a Cr column. Assets and expenses are debit balances. Liabilities, capital and income (such as sales) are credit balances. If the two columns are equal, the arithmetic of the ledgers is consistent; this does not prove that no error was made (for example an error of omission or a compensating error can still balance).

Check of the original first-method example (Madam Cash Nig. Ltd): cash book Dr side 950 + 7,000 + 2,000 = 9,950; Cr side 3,200 + 400 + 200 = 3,800; balance c/d 6,150. Trial balance: Dr Motor van 3,200 + Salary 400 + Wages 200 + Cash 6,150 = 9,950; Cr Capital 950 + Sales 9,000 = 9,950. It balances. Note: the original question says "as at July, 2005" but the title says "as at 30 July, 2008"; the year cannot be recovered and does not affect the figures.

Correction to the original second-method example: the printed table lost the label "Building". The amount 2000 appears in the heading row beside "Particular". Restored trial balance: Dr Building 2,000; Equipment 5,000; Stock 1,000; Motor van 3,000 = 11,000. Cr Capital 2,000; Creditor 7,000; Accrued 2,000 = 11,000. Without Building the debit column would add to only 9,000.

Practice questions: Tunde started business on Mar. 1 with N10,000 cash; Mar. 4 bought furniture N3,000 cash; Mar. 8 cash sales N6,000; Mar. 12 paid rent N1,000 cash. (a) Find the cash balance. (b) Prepare the trial balance.

Answers and marking guide: (a) 10,000 + 6,000 - 3,000 - 1,000 = 12,000 (debit balance). (b) Dr: Furniture 3,000; Rent 1,000; Cash 12,000; total 16,000. Cr: Capital 10,000; Sales 6,000; total 16,000. One mark per correct line and one for equal totals.

title: Trading and profit and loss account: worked answer for babasuwe Nig. Ltd
body:
Objectives: prepare a trading account and a profit and loss account from a list of balances; calculate net sales, cost of goods sold, gross profit and net profit.

Teaching: Net sales = sales - return inward. Cost of goods available = opening stock + purchases - return outward (add carriage inward if given). Cost of goods sold = goods available - closing stock. Gross profit = net sales - cost of goods sold. In the profit and loss account, gross profit and other income (discount received) go on the credit side; expenses (rent, insurance, electricity, discount allowed) go on the debit side; net profit is the balancing figure. The original layout writes "sales return" where the notes define "return inward"; they are the same item.

Worked answer to the original assignment (babasuwe Nig. Ltd, 31 Dec. 2008): Net sales = 10,000 - 150 = 9,850. Goods available = 2,000 + 2,000 - 100 = 3,900. Cost of goods sold = 3,900 - 1,000 = 2,900. Gross profit = 9,850 - 2,900 = 6,950. Expenses = rent 500 + insurance 600 + electricity 300 + discount allowed 200 = 1,600. Income = 6,950 + 400 = 7,350. Net profit = 7,350 - 1,600 = 5,750. Trading account totals 9,850 each side; profit and loss account totals 7,350 each side. No wages figure is given in the assignment, so none is entered.

Practice questions: Sales 8,000; opening stock 1,000; purchases 3,000; return outward 200; return inward 300; closing stock 800; rent 400; discount received 100. Prepare the trading and profit and loss account.

Answers and marking guide: net sales 7,700; goods available 3,800; cost of goods sold 3,000; gross profit 4,700; income 4,700 + 100 = 4,800; expenses 400; net profit 4,400. Trading account totals 7,700; profit and loss totals 4,800. One mark per correct subtotal and one for each balanced account.

title: International A-series paper sizes: corrected table for keyboarding
body:
Objectives: state the A-series sizes in millimetres; explain the halving rule; choose the correct page dimensions for a display exercise.

Teaching: Each A size is made by halving the previous size across its longer side, so A4 folded once gives A5. Correct sizes (width x length): A1 594 x 841; A2 420 x 594; A3 297 x 420; A4 210 x 297; A5 148 x 210; A6 105 x 148; A7 74 x 105. Correction to the original note: it prints A4 as 219mm x 297mm; the correct width is 210mm. The original lists A2 as 594 x 420, which is the same sheet turned sideways (landscape). Foolscap, Six Mo, Quarto and Octavo sizes in the original are older formats and are left as printed. The landscape/portrait numbers in the original second table have no stated unit or meaning, so they are not explained here.

A5 landscape means the long side runs across: 210mm wide and 148mm tall. The menu exercise in the original lesson uses A5 landscape.

Practice questions: (a) What is half of A3? (b) What are the dimensions of A5 in landscape? (c) Which printed A4 width in the original note is wrong?

Answers and marking guide: (a) A4, 210 x 297. (b) 210mm wide by 148mm tall. (c) 219mm; it should be 210mm. One mark each.
